name: Controlled Vocabulary
contentMarkdown:
# Controlled Vocabulary

A controlled vocabulary is a managed set of terms used to describe and organize information consistently. It defines which terms to use, what they mean, and, where useful, how synonyms and related concepts connect.

In product design, it can support navigation labels, metadata, filters, search, and documentation. W3C's SKOS provides a model for representing concepts, preferred and alternative labels, and relationships between concepts.

## Example: booking statuses

Suppose teams use “confirmed,” “booked,” and “ticketed” inconsistently. A controlled vocabulary could define:

| Term | Meaning in this product |
|---|---|
| Confirmed | The supplier has confirmed the reservation. |
| Ticketed | A ticket has been issued. |
| Canceled | The reservation has been canceled. |

The definitions matter because “confirmed” and “ticketed” describe different states in this example. They should not be merged merely because users sometimes treat them as synonyms.

A separate search alias could help users who type “cancelled” find records labeled “Canceled.” Keep display labels separate from stable internal identifiers.

## How to keep it useful

Start with terms that affect actual tasks. Record each term's definition, scope, accepted alternatives, and owner. Check the language with users and domain experts.

Map the vocabulary to interface labels, content fields, and search behavior. Establish how proposed terms are reviewed and how deprecated terms are redirected or migrated.

A vocabulary can provide consistent labels for AI retrieval and outputs when the application uses it. It does not ensure that a model will interpret every term correctly. Test ambiguous queries and preserve the original meaning when translating or summarizing content.

name: Faceted Classification
contentMarkdown:
# Faceted Classification

Faceted classification organizes items by several dimensions, called facets, that users can combine when finding information. A travel product might classify flights by airline, number of stops, departure time, and cabin.

## How do facets work?

Each item has values for the facets relevant to it. Faceted navigation exposes those values as filters. The product must define how selections combine and how counts change as the result set narrows.

## Example: Narrowing flight results

A traveler selects Nonstop, Morning departure, and either Airline A or Airline B. In this example, the system combines different facets with AND and the two airlines with OR. Results must satisfy all three dimensions while matching either selected airline.

Show selected filters, make them removable, and update counts consistently with the chosen logic. If no flights match, identify the active constraints and provide a way to relax them. The exact combination rules should follow the product’s data and users’ expectations.

## What should teams model and test?

Use research to choose dimensions people actually use to decide. Define consistent values and handling for missing data. Avoid presenting two labels for the same cabin category unless the distinction matters.

Test a realistic search from a broad result set to a suitable option. Check whether users understand the labels, selected states, counts, and effect of clearing a filter. Faceted classification depends on maintained metadata as well as a usable filter interface.

## Related terms

- [Information Architecture (IA)](/glossary/information-architecture.html)
- [Polyhierarchy](/glossary/polyhierarchy.html)
- [Content Modeling](/glossary/content-modeling.html)

## Sources

- [Filters vs. Facets, Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/filters-vs-facets/)

name: Task Model
contentMarkdown:
# Task Model

A task model is a structured description of the activities people perform to achieve a goal, including subtasks, decisions, dependencies, and relevant conditions. Designers use it to understand the work an interface needs to support.

Task models can range from a simple hierarchy to a formal representation of task relationships. Their value comes from accurately describing the work and its constraints.

## Example: approving an invoice

The goal is to approve a valid invoice for payment. A simplified model might include:

1. Find invoices awaiting review.
2. Check the supplier, amount, and purchase order.
3. Resolve missing information or discrepancies.
4. Approve within the reviewer's authority, or route to an authorized approver.
5. Confirm that the invoice has moved to the correct state.

The model should include exceptions: the invoice may be a duplicate, the purchase order may be missing, or the reviewer may lack approval authority. Some checks can happen independently; approval depends on the required checks being complete.

These relationships inform interface requirements such as visible status, supporting documents, and a clear handoff.

## How to build one

Observe people doing the work and ask about decisions, workarounds, and failures. Identify the goal before documenting the steps. Validate the model with people who actually perform the task.

A user flow describes a route through an interface. A task model can describe work across screens, tools, or offline activities, including work that the future product will support differently.

Use the model to test whether the design covers the task's conditions and recovery paths. Update it when responsibilities or business rules change.

## Related terms

- [Jobs to Be Done (JTBD)](/glossary/jobs-to-be-done-jtbd.html)
- [Mental Model Mapping](/glossary/mental-model-mapping.html)
- [Service Blueprinting](/glossary/service-blueprinting.html)

## Sources

- [Nielsen Norman Group: Task Analysis](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/task-analysis/)
- [W3C: Task Models](https://www.w3.org/TR/task-models/)

name: Wayfinding System
contentMarkdown:
# Wayfinding System

A wayfinding system is a set of cues that helps people understand where they are, where they can go, and how to return to a useful starting point. In digital products, those cues include page titles, current-section indicators, breadcrumbs, and clearly labeled destinations.

## What does digital wayfinding include?

| User question | Interface cue |
|---|---|
| Where am I? | A descriptive page title, the name of the current record, and a visible current-section indicator. |
| Where can I go? | Navigation labels and links that explain which information or action is available. |
| How do I get back? | A route to the parent section or a return link that restores the user’s previous task context. |

Information architecture defines the structure that these cues help users navigate. Breadcrumbs show a location within that hierarchy. For a linear process, a step indicator can show how far the user has progressed.

## Example: Returning from an invoice to a booking list

An operations agent opens Booking #1042 from a filtered list and then views its invoice. The invoice page identifies the document and booking. A breadcrumb offers a route back to the booking. A “Back to booking results” link restores the previous filters and page.

Each cue answers a question the agent encounters during the task. A status such as “Refund pending” provides additional context, and the Invoice title makes the current document clear.

## How do you test a wayfinding system?

Ask users to enter through a deep link, identify what they are viewing, and find a related record. Then ask them to return to the list they were working from. Observe whether titles and labels help, whether return links preserve useful state, and where users lose their place. Repeat the task in the narrow-screen layout, where some navigation may collapse into a menu.

- [Semantic Zoom](/glossary/semantic-zoom.html)

name: Semantic Zoom
contentMarkdown:
# Semantic Zoom

Semantic zoom changes the information or representation shown at different levels of scale. It lets users move between an overview and meaningful detail while retaining a connection to the same underlying content.

For example, a planning view might show monthly totals at one level, daily groups at another, and individual bookings at a detailed level. Optical zoom changes magnification; semantic zoom changes what is represented.

Microsoft's SemanticZoom control is a specific implementation that switches between two related views of grouped content. The broader design concept can involve more than two levels.

## Example: a hotel planning board

At the overview level, a manager sees occupancy by week. Selecting a week reveals daily room availability. Opening a day shows the reservations behind its totals.

The transition should preserve the selected date and explain where the user is. Returning to the overview should make it easy to recognize the same period.

Use consistent calculations so a summary can be reconciled with its detail. If filters change the totals, show the active scope.

## When it helps

Semantic zoom can help when users need both broad patterns and record-level work. It is less useful when extra levels only add navigation to a short list.

Define the questions each level answers and the information users need to decide where to go next.

## Accessibility checks

Provide an operable way to move between levels without relying on a pinch gesture alone. Preserve logical focus, meaningful labels, and an understandable reading order.

For web products, keep browser text resizing available. Semantic zoom is an application interaction and does not replace the user's need to enlarge text.
